propositions.text: Christian converts in Iran face persecution and death penalty as apostasy is punishable by death under Iranian law.
propositions.quote: The situation of Christian converts in Iran is grave. They face persecution by the authorities and even punishment by death: The constitution does not provide for the rights of Muslim citizens to choose, change, or renounce their religious beliefs. The government considers a child born to a Muslim father to be a Muslim and deems conversion from Islam to be apostasy, which is punishable by death.

propositions.text: Christian converts face physical attacks, harassment, surveillance, arrest, detention, torture and ill-treatment in Iran.
propositions.quote: Christian converts face physical attacks, harassment, surveillance, arrest, detention, as well as torture and ill-treatment in detention.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Christian converts in Iran face persecution, death penalty, and physical abuse under Iranian law and practice.

propositions.text: Apostasy is punishable by death in Iran and Christians face risk of ill-treatment or torture during incarceration before court hearings.
propositions.quote: Apostasy is punishable by death. Moreover, even if Christians and Christian converts have been released in Iran without having been charged, a danger of persecution still exists for them: By the time the case goes to court, or the accused may be released without charges, there will have been a substantial risk of ill-treatment or torture while in incarceration.

paragraphs.summary: The court states apostasy is punishable by death and Christians risk ill-treatment or torture during incarceration in Iran.

propositions.text: This is an application for judicial review of a Senior Immigration Officer's decision rejecting the Applicant's PRRA application.
propositions.quote: This is an application for judicial review pursuant to subsection 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA] of the decision of a Senior Immigration Officer [Officer], dated February 27, 2015, rejecting the Applicant’s pre-removal risk assessment [PRRA] application.

paragraphs.summary: The court introduces the judicial review application of the Senior Immigration Officer's PRRA decision rejecting the Applicant's application.

propositions.text: The Applicant, Monir Darvishpour Hassankiadeh, is a 59-year-old Iranian citizen.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, Monir Darvishpour Hassankiadeh (age 59), is a citizen of Iran.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant is Monir Darvishpour Hassankiadeh, a 59-year-old Iranian citizen.

propositions.text: Applicant and daughter converted from Islam to Christianity after daughter's coma and traumatic events.
propositions.quote: The Applicant alleged in front of the Refugee Protection Division [RPD] of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada that she and her daughter converted from Islam to Christianity after her daughter awoke from a coma in 2003 subsequent to her daughter’s attempted suicide after she was detained and raped.

propositions.text: Applicant and daughter made multiple unsuccessful attempts to come to Canada after conversion.
propositions.quote: The Applicant and her daughter attempted, on a number of occasions, to come to Canada after their conversion to Christianity: i) in 2004, the application to obtain visitors visas for her family was rejected; ii) her daughter applied the following summer for a student visa without success; iii) in 2006, a new application to obtain visitors visas for the family was rejected; iv) later in 2006, the Applicant’s daughter entered into a marriage with an Iranian-Canadian for the purpose of gaining status in Canada subsequent to having undergone traumatic experiences in Iran.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant alleges she and her daughter converted to Christianity after trauma and made multiple failed attempts to come to Canada.

propositions.text: Applicant's daughter arrived in Canada in 2009 via fraudulent marriage and filed refugee claim in 2010; Applicant arrived in 2011 and joined claim.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s daughter arrived in Canada in April 2009 on the basis of the fraudulent marriage. Unable to obtain Canadian status through the marriage, the Applicant’s daughter filed a refugee claim in May 2010. The Applicant arrived in Canada in January 2011 to visit her older daughter who is both Canadian and Iranian citizen. The Applicant made a claim for refugee protection in October 2011, and her claim was joined to that of her daughter.

propositions.text: RPD rejected Applicant and daughter's refugee claims, finding they are not genuine Christian converts due to vague, evasive, inconsistent testimony.
propositions.quote: In a decision dated September 14, 2012, the RPD rejected the Applicant and her daughter’s refugee claims finding that the Applicant and her daughter are not genuine converts to Christianity. Specifically, the RPD found the Applicant’s testimony was frequently vague, evasive and punctuated by a theatrical demonstration when speaking of religious matters and that the Applicant’s evidence was riddled with inconsistency and contradiction.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant's daughter came to Canada via fraudulent marriage and filed refugee claim; RPD rejected claims as not genuine converts due to credibility issues.

propositions.text: Applicant filed first PRRA in 2013 without counsel, rejected in 2014; judicial review settled; PRRA reconsidered and rejected in 2015.
propositions.quote: In October 2013, the Applicant filed, without the assistance of counsel, an application for PRRA. This first application for PRRA was rejected in May 2014. The Applicant made an application for judicial review to this Court (IMM‑5461‑14), but the parties settled and agreed that the PRRA application would be reconsidered. The Applicant submitted considerable substantial new evidence with submissions and, after reconsideration, the Officer rejected the Applicant’s PRRA application in a decision dated February 27, 2015 [Application].

paragraphs.summary: Applicant filed first PRRA in 2013 rejected in 2014; judicial review settled; PRRA reconsidered and rejected in 2015.

propositions.text: Officer found Applicant not at risk of persecution or torture if returned to Iran and gave no weight to new evidence contradicting RPD credibility findings.
propositions.quote: In his decision, the Officer found that the Applicant would not be subject to risk of persecution, danger or torture, risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if she was to return to Iran. The Officer gave no weight to the new evidence, such as, the affidavits, letters, photographs, country condition documents, and medical report submitted by the Applicant as they did not contradict the findings of the RPD regarding the credibility of the Applicant.

propositions.text: Officer found Applicant's conversion not shown to be genuine conviction, affidavits only showed participation, not motivation.
propositions.quote: Particularly, the Officer found that the Applicant did not submit sufficient evidence that the Applicant’s conversion to Christianity in Canada is one of conviction and not one of convenience, this subsequent to affidavits from two pastors and a reverend which the Officer held were only to attest to the Applicant’s participation in church activities and not to her motivations.

propositions.text: Officer found Applicant did not show sufficient evidence of persecution risk in Iran.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the Officer found that the Applicant had not submitted sufficient evidence to demonstrate that she would be persecuted in Iran.

propositions.text: Officer found Applicant not at risk due to refugee claim in Canada as Iranian authorities do not receive such information during removal process.
propositions.quote: Finally, the Officer found that the Applicant is not at risk of persecution simply because she made a refugee claim in Canada, noting that at no point during the removal process from Canada, do Iranian authorities or other foreign jurisdictions receive information formally that an individual has made a refugee claim in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found Applicant not at risk if returned, gave no weight to new evidence, found conversion not genuine, and no risk from refugee claim.

propositions.text: IRPA sections 96 and 97 define Convention refugee and person in need of protection with criteria for persecution and risk.
propositions.quote: The following are the relevant legislative provisions of the IRPA: Convention refugee Définition de « réfugié » 96. A Convention refugee is a person who, by reason of a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group or political opinion, 96. A qualité de réfugié au sens de la Convention — le réfugié — la personne qui, craignant avec raison d’être persécutée du fait de sa race, de sa religion, de sa nationalité, de son appartenance à un groupe social ou de ses opinions politiques : (a) is outside each of their countries of nationality and is unable or, by reason of that fear, unwilling to avail themself of the protection of each of those countries; or a) soit se trouve hors de tout pays dont elle a la nationalité et ne peut ou, du fait de cette crainte, ne veut se réclamer de la protection de chacun de ces pays.

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRPA sections 96 and 97 define Convention refugee and person in need of protection criteria.

propositions.text: Applicant argues Officer erred by dismissing expert evidence, ignoring new evidence on faith, dismissing Pastor Tabiany's affidavit, wrongly finding no risk as failed refugee claimant, and breaching procedural fairness by denying oral hearing.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the Officer committed several reviewable errors, specifically: the Officer erred in dismissing the expert evidence; he failed to consider the new evidence related to the genuineness of the Applicant’s Christian faith and practice; he erred in giving no weight to the affidavit of Pastor Tabiany; he erred in finding that the Applicant is not at risk as a failed refugee claimant; and, that the Officer breached his duty in respect of procedural fairness by refusing to hold an oral hearing.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submits Officer erred by dismissing evidence, ignoring new faith evidence, dismissing affidavit, wrongly finding no risk, and breaching fairness by denying oral hearing.

propositions.text: Respondent argues PRRA is not an appeal of RPD decision and Officer reasonably found new evidence insufficient to contradict RPD credibility findings.
propositions.quote: Conversely, the Respondent submits that the PRRA is not an appeal of the RPD’s determination. The Officer further submits that it was reasonable for him to find that the new evidence submitted by the Applicant in support of her PRRA application was not sufficient to contradict the RPD’s findings that the Applicant was not credible.

propositions.text: Respondent argues it was reasonable to give little weight to expert opinion relying on facts deemed not credible by RPD.
propositions.quote: According to the Respondent, it was also reasonable for the Officer to give little weight to the expert opinion as the expert opinion relied on facts that were deemed not to be credible by the RPD.

propositions.text: Respondent argues it was reasonable to reject pastors' affidavits as they did not address Applicant's vague, evasive testimony and church attendance credibility issues.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that it was also reasonable for the Officer to reject the affidavits of the pastors and the reverend as they did not address the vague, evasive and contradictory testimony of the Applicant before the RPD; that, especially, in light of the Applicant’s testimony that the RPD found to lack credibility in respect of the Applicant’s attendance of protestant-Christian church services in Iran, as the RPD concluded that churches are not monitored by the Iranian authorities.

propositions.text: Respondent argues oral hearing not required as PRRA officers hold them only in exceptional cases, which this case does not meet.
propositions.quote: Regarding the issue of an oral hearing, the Respondent submits that it is not required. The PRRA officer only holds oral in-person hearings in exceptional cases, and this case did not warrant an oral hearing as all the criteria set out at section 113(b) of the IRPA were not met.

propositions.text: Respondent argues Officer's finding no risk from refugee claim is reasonable as Applicant failed to prove link between personal circumstances and Iran conditions.
propositions.quote: Finally, the Respondent submits that the Officer’s findings that the Applicant would not be at risk in Iran due to her refugee claim in Canada is reasonable as the Applicant had not satisfied her burden of proof by establishing a link between her personal circumstances and country conditions in Iran.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues PRRA is not appeal, Officer reasonably found evidence insufficient, rejected affidavits, oral hearing not required, and no risk from refugee claim.

propositions.text: Standard of review of reasonableness applies to PRRA Officers' fact and law determinations (Nebie v Canada).
propositions.quote: The standard of review of reasonableness is applicable wherein fact and law determinations as well as fact determinations are reached by PRRA Officers (Nebie v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 701).

paragraphs.summary: The court states reasonableness standard applies to PRRA Officers' fact and law determinations.

propositions.text: Reasonableness standard applies to Immigration Officers' decisions on oral hearing rights, with deference (Ndagijimana; Matano).
propositions.quote: The determinations of Immigration Officers, such as PRRA decision-makers, in respect of the rights to oral hearings must also be reviewed under the standard of reasonableness as it is a core element of the officers’ jurisdiction and is a matter to which the Court owes considerable deference to the officer (Ndagijimana v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 43; Matano v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 1290).

paragraphs.summary: The court states reasonableness standard applies to Immigration Officers' oral hearing decisions with deference.

propositions.text: Whether the Officer’s PRRA decision is reasonable is the central issue for judicial review.
propositions.quote: The central issue to be determined by this application for judicial review is whether the Officer’s PRRA decision is reasonable.

propositions.text: The court finds the Officer’s decision unreasonable after reviewing submissions and evidence.
propositions.quote: This Court finds, after a careful review of the submissions of the parties as well as a thorough examination of all the evidence, that the Officer’s decision is unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the central issue is reasonableness of Officer's decision and finds it unreasonable after review.

propositions.text: PRRA purpose is to allow removal order subjects to apply for protection; granted if applicant meets Convention refugee or person in need of protection definitions.
propositions.quote: The purpose of a PRRA is undisputed; it is to allow a person that is subject to a removal order to apply for protection (Raza v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 385 at para 10 [Raza]; section 112 of the IRPA). Succinctly, a PRRA application will be granted – subject to restrictions regarding criminality or national security – if at the time of the PRRA application the Applicant meets the definition of a “Convention refugee” at section 96 of the IRPA or the definition of a “person in need of protection” at section 97 of the IRPA (Raza, above at para 11; section 112 of the IRPA). A successful PRRA application will have the effect of conferring refugee protection to its applicant (subsection 114(1) of the IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The court states PRRA allows removal order subjects to apply for protection if meeting refugee or protection definitions under IRPA.

propositions.text: PRRA is not an appeal of RPD decision; Officer must defer to RPD unless new evidence arises (Singh; Elezi).
propositions.quote: It is well established that a PRRA is not an appeal mechanism of a negative RPD decision; and, the PRRA Officer must give deference to the RPD’s determination of the claim; however, the Officer must examine whether new facts or evidence have come to light since the RPD’s rejection of the claim: [50] A PRRA officer is not a quasi-judicial body, nor does he or she have an appellate function when faced with a RPD decision. The PRRA officer is an employee of the Minister, acting within his or her employer's discretion (insofar as it is circumscribed by the Act and the Regulations). The PRRA officer must give deference to the RPD's determination of the claim, to the extent that the facts remain unchanged from the time it had rendered its decision. Instead, the PRRA officer is specifically looking as to whether new evidence has come to light since the RPD's rejection of the claim for determining a risk of persecution, a danger of torture, a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. The underlying rationale for paragraph 113(a) of the Act is not appellate in nature but rather to assure the claimant has a last chance to have any new risks of refoulement (not previously assessed by the RPD) assessed before removal can take place. [My emphasis.] (Singh v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 1022 at para 50; see also Elezi v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FC 240 at para 27)

paragraphs.summary: The court states PRRA is not an appeal of RPD decision; Officer must defer unless new evidence arises.

propositions.text: Iranian Constitution protects religious minorities in theory but Christians face discrimination and persecution in practice.
propositions.quote: While it is true, in theory, that religious minorities are protected pursuant to the Iranian Constitution, it is not the case in practice. As demonstrated by the objective documentary evidence, it is unequivocal that Christians in Iran have been targeted by the authorities and are at risk of discrimination and are at risk of persecution: The Iranian Constitution recognises Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians as protected religious minorities. However the state does discriminate against them on the basis of religion or belief, as all laws and regulations are based on unique Shi’a Islamic criteria. It is difficult for many Christians to live freely and openly in Iran. Such discrimination is prevalent throughout Iran.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Iranian Constitution protects minorities in theory but Christians face discrimination and persecution in practice.

propositions.text: Christian converts in Iran face persecution, death penalty, and physical abuse under Sharia law and government policy.
propositions.quote: The situation is even more problematic for Christian converts in Iran who face persecution by the authorities and even punishment by death: The constitution does not provide for the rights of Muslim citizens to choose, change, or renounce their religious beliefs. The government considers a child born to a Muslim father to be a Muslim and deems conversion from Islam to be apostasy, which is punishable by death. [My emphasis.] (U.S. Department of State, International Religious Freedom Report for 2014, Iran) Christians who have converted from Islam are at risk of harm from the state authorities, as they are considered apostates – a criminal offence in Iran. Sharia law does not allow for conversion from Islam to another religion, and it is not possible for an individual person to change their religious affiliation on personal documentation. Christian converts face physical attacks, harassment, surveillance, arrest, detention, as well as torture and ill-treatment in detention. [My emphasis.] (United Kingdom: Home Office, Country Information and Guidance – Iran: Christians and Christian Converts, December 2014 at section 1.3.3)

paragraphs.summary: The court states Christian converts in Iran face persecution, death penalty, and physical abuse under Sharia law and government policy.

propositions.text: Applicant must demonstrate well-founded fear or personalized risk under IRPA sections 96 or 97, not just general risk in Iran.
propositions.quote: As problematic as the situation is for Christian converts in Iran, it is trite law that it is insufficient for a PRRA applicant to simply state that there is a risk in Iran, an applicant has to demonstrate that they have a well-founded fear under section 96 of the IRPA or that they established a personalized risk under section 97 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Applicant must show well-founded fear or personalized risk under IRPA, not just general risk in Iran.

propositions.text: It was unreasonable for Officer to reject affidavits of pastors and reverend based on participation not motivation.
propositions.quote: It was unreasonable for the Officer to reject the affidavits of Pastor Siroos Tabiany of Persian Christian Fellowship and Pastor Hany Boghossian of the Well on Bayview as well as of Reverend Terry Thom of St. Matthew’s United Church. In his decision, the Officer stated that he relied on the credibility findings of the RPD to determine that the Applicant is a Christian out of convenience rather that of belief. The Officer rejected the affidavits of the Pastors and the Reverend as the affidavits only discussed the Applicant’s participation in their churches activities and not her motivations as to why she became a Christian.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it unreasonable for Officer to reject pastors' affidavits based on participation not motivation.

propositions.text: Officer must examine new facts or evidence showing new risks since RPD's determination.
propositions.quote: the Officer owes deference to the findings of the RPD, he has an obligation to examine whether new facts or evidence have come to light demonstrating that new risks have arisen since the RPD’s determination.

propositions.text: Officer rejected affidavits of Pastors and Reverend based on RPD's credibility findings and lack of training in credibility assessment.
propositions.quote: the Officer rejected all the affidavits of the Pastors and the Reverend on the basis of the credibility findings of the RPD that the Applicant is not a genuine Christian; that the affidavits do not speak of the motivations of the Applicant; and, that the assessment of the Pastors and the Reverend may not substitute the assessment of the RPD as they are not trained in assessing the credibility of an individual.

propositions.text: RPD did not have new evidence of affidavits from clergy members from various churches.
propositions.quote: the RPD did not have the new evidence of the several affidavits of members of the clergy from various churches.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Officer must examine new evidence of risks since RPD's decision; Officer rejected clergy affidavits based on RPD's findings; RPD lacked new clergy affidavits.

propositions.text: Officer must assess if Applicant is currently a genuine Christian, not rely solely on RPD's pre-determination findings.
propositions.quote: the Officer had the obligation to assess whether the Applicant is currently a genuine Christian. This determination cannot be made solely on relying on the findings of the RPD as the RPD’s findings are based on whether the Applicant genuinely converted to Christianity pre the RPD’s determination.

propositions.text: UNHCR Guidelines state post-departure conversion may create a sur place claim even if decision-maker doubts genuineness.
propositions.quote: a conversion post departure may have the effect of creating a sur place claim – this is even possible if the decision-maker is not satisfied that the Applicant is a genuine believer: 36.

propositions.text: Self-serving activities do not create well-founded fear if opportunistic nature is apparent and no serious adverse consequences result.
propositions.quote: So-called “self-serving” activities do not create a well-founded fear of persecution on a Convention ground in the claimant’s country of origin, if the opportunistic nature of such activities will be apparent to all, including the authorities there, and serious adverse consequences would not result if the person were returned.

propositions.text: Consider consequences of return and potential harm for refugee status or protection even if claim is self-serving.
propositions.quote: consideration must be given as to the consequences of return to the country of origin and any potential harm that might justify refugee status or a complementary form of protection.

propositions.text: If claim is self-serving but claimant has well-founded fear of persecution, international protection is required.
propositions.quote: In the event that the claim is found to be self-serving but the claimant nonetheless has a well-founded fear of persecution on return, international protection is required.

propositions.text: Opportunistic nature weighs on durable solutions and residency status.
propositions.quote: Where the opportunistic nature of the action is clearly apparent, however, this could weigh heavily in the balance when considering potential durable solutions that may be available in such cases, as well as, for example, the type of residency status.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Officer must assess current genuineness of Christianity; cites UNHCR Guidelines on sur place claims and self-serving activities.

propositions.text: Officer rejected Pastor Tabiany's affidavit despite RPD finding him credible after testimony.
propositions.quote: the Officer rejected the affidavit of Pastor Tabiany, who the RPD had determined, subsequent to having heard his testimony, that he was credible;

propositions.text: Officer found Pastor not trained in assessing credibility or faith genuineness, so Pastor's assessment cannot substitute RPD's.
propositions.quote: the Officer found the Pastor is not trained in assessing credibility nor the genuineness of a person’s faith, the RPD determined that the Pastor’s assessment cannot be substituted for that of the RPD

propositions.text: Pastor Tabiany regularly interacted with Applicant and assessed her faith genuineness for years.
propositions.quote: Pastor Tabiany has had the opportunity to interact with the Applicant on a regular basis and assess the genuineness of her faith for years.

propositions.text: RPD found Pastor Tabiany credible, so his testimony is substantially significant.
propositions.quote: Based on the RPD’s findings that Pastor Tabiany is a credible witness, it cannot be said that his testimony is not substantially significant.

propositions.text: Unreasonable to reject Pastor Tabiany's affidavit without weight or careful review by PRRA.
propositions.quote: it was unreasonable to simply reject the affidavit of Pastor Tabiany and not give it any weight.

propositions.text: PRRA must carefully review clergy affidavits and consider them, even if not bound by Pastor's testimony.
propositions.quote: the PRRA still had the obligation to carefully review the information contained in the affidavit by Pastor Tabiany and that of other members of the clergy; and, at the very least, to take that into consideration.

propositions.text: Officer could not reject Pastor Tabiany's opinion on Christian beliefs and activities without careful review.
propositions.quote: The Officer could not simply reject it without carefully reviewing Pastor Tabiany’s opinion in respect of the Christian beliefs and activities as described by Pastor Tabiany in his affidavit.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it unreasonable for Officer to reject Pastor Tabiany's credible affidavit without careful review and consideration by PRRA.

propositions.text: Officer's decision is unreasonable for relying solely on RPD findings to assess current genuineness of Christianity.
propositions.quote: The Court finds that the Officer’s decision is unreasonable; the Officer could not rely solely on the findings of the RPD to assess whether the Applicant is currently a genuine Christian

propositions.text: Unreasonable for Officer to give no weight to affidavits of Pastors and Reverend, especially Pastor Tabiany's affidavit.
propositions.quote: it was unreasonable for the Officer to give no weight to the affidavits of the Pastors and the Reverend, specifically to that of the affidavit of Pastor Tabiany.

propositions.text: UNHCR Guidelines require international protection if well-founded fear of persecution exists despite self-serving conversion.
propositions.quote: even if the Applicant’s conversion is, in and of itself, found to be self-serving but that the Applicant does have a well-founded fear of persecution, then international protection is required

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Officer's decision is unreasonable for ignoring new evidence and UNHCR Guidelines on protection despite self-serving conversion.

propositions.text: Officer found Applicant not at risk if returned to Iran due to no known anti-government activities.
propositions.quote: The Officer found that the Applicant would not be at risk as a result of her refugee claim in Canada if she returns to Iran, as the Applicant is not known to have been implicated in anti-government activities

propositions.text: Officer's determination is unreasonable given objective documentary evidence of monitoring and harassment of apostates in Iran.
propositions.quote: This determination by the Officer is unreasonable as clear, unequivocal, objective documentary evidence suggests otherwise.

propositions.text: Iranians committing apostasy are monitored by authorities; church groups face state monitoring and harassment.
propositions.quote: Iranians who have committed apostasy are carefully monitored by the Iranian authorities: Church groups are routinely subjected to state monitoring and harassment in Iran.

propositions.text: Ministry of Intelligence and others summon church leaders for questioning and coerce information about church activities and members.
propositions.quote: The Ministry of Intelligence, Police or Revolutionary Courts would summon church leaders for questioning and try to coerce them into providing information about church activities, services, education programs and the names and backgrounds of church members.

propositions.text: Christians report intelligence officers follow them and tap phones; info leads to arrests and church closures.
propositions.quote: Christians also reported to the ICHRI that intelligence officers told them they were following them and tapping their phones. The information gathered by the Ministry of Intelligence then becomes the basis for arrests, prosecutions and the closure of churches.

propositions.text: UK Home Office report documents monitoring and harassment of Christians in Iran.
propositions.quote: (United Kingdom: Home Office, Country Information and Guidance – Iran: Christians and Christian Converts, December 2014 at section 2.6.9)

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Officer's no-risk finding unreasonable given evidence of Iranian monitoring and harassment of apostates and Christians.

propositions.text: Apostasy is punishable by death in Iran.
propositions.quote: Apostasy is punishable by death.

propositions.text: Even if released without charges, converts face risk of ill-treatment or torture during incarceration.
propositions.quote: even if Christians and Christian converts have been released in Iran without having been charged, a danger of persecution still exist for them: By the time the case goes to court, or the accused may be released without charges, there will have been a substantial risk of ill-treatment or torture while in incarceration.

propositions.text: Risk of harm from arrest to court hearing should not be underestimated.
propositions.quote: It should not be underestimated what can happen from the time of arrest up until a court hearing.

propositions.text: Danish Immigration Service report on situation for Christian converts in Iran.
propositions.quote: (Danish Immigration Service, Updated on the Situation for Christian Converts in Iran, June 2014, at part 1.2.2 Iranian legislation and cases against converts)

paragraphs.summary: The court cites reports that apostasy is punishable by death and converts face risk of ill-treatment or torture in Iran.

propositions.text: Officer's finding that Applicant is not in peril or at risk if returned to Iran is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: it was unreasonable for the Officer to find that the Applicant is not, as a failed refugee claimant, in peril if she is to return to Iran and that she would not be at risk if discovered by the authorities as a Christian convert who committed apostasy.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Officer's finding of no peril or risk to Applicant if returned to Iran is unreasonable.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review is granted; file sent back to different PRRA officer for new assessment.
propositions.quote: the application for judicial review be granted. The file be sent back to a different PRRA officer for assessment anew.

propositions.text: No serious question of general importance to be certified.
propositions.quote: There is no serious question of general importance to be certified.

paragraphs.summary: The court grants judicial review, remands file to different PRRA officer, and declines to certify serious question of general importance.
